title: Here am I; send me (Isaiah 6:1–8)
hook: seraphim, a live coal on the lips, and a prophet who volunteers

segments.voice: Yesterday, a forge, and your line: war is learned, and unlearned. Today, the scene many readers take as Isaiah's call.

"In the year that king Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and His train filled the temple." Isaiah dates the vision by a death. A king is gone, and in the Temple a man sees something that fills the whole space. Above the throne stand seraphim, burning ones, each with six wings: two to cover the face, two to cover the feet, two to fly. And they are calling to one another.
screen: `THE YEAR KING UZZIAH DIED.` → `HIGH AND LIFTED UP.` → `SERAPHIM CALLING.`

segments.voice: What they call is this: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; The whole earth is full of His glory." You may have heard it in a synagogue. It's at the heart of the Kedushah, said during the leader's repetition of the Amidah, when people rise up on their toes at each holy. The doorposts shake. Smoke fills the house. And Isaiah's first words aren't brave at all: "Woe is me! for I am undone; Because I am a man of unclean lips, And I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips". He feels too small and too stained for the room. Then one of the seraphim takes a live coal from the altar with tongs, flies to him, and touches his mouth: "Lo, this hath touched thy lips; And thine iniquity is taken away". The lips he was ashamed of are the ones cleansed, the very place a prophet will work. Then Isaiah hears a voice, not addressed to him, a question into the room: "Whom shall I send, And who will go for us?" And he answers: "Here am I; send me." In Hebrew, the first word is hineni. Abraham says hineni when God calls him by name. So does Moses at the burning bush. But they were called by name. Isaiah wasn't. He heard an open question and stepped forward, and said yes before he heard the job. The task that follows is a hard one, as the very next verses show. Hineni is not a promise that it'll be easy. It's a person saying: I'm here, I'm listening, use me.
screen: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `WOE IS ME, A MAN OF UNCLEAN LIPS.` · `A LIVE COAL TOUCHES HIS LIPS.` · then, large: `HERE AM I; SEND ME.`

segments.voice: Listen for the open questions around you that nobody's answering: who can drive, who'll bring food, who'll sit with her? If a voice in you says, like Isaiah, I'm not good enough for this, breathe through it, and quietly try the word: hineni, here I am. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
Hineni. "Here I am": Isaiah's answer to an open question in the Temple, given before he knew the task. Today's word.
Your line: here am I, send me. Said before he even knew the task. Rest well.

howItsDone: Jews say the seraphim's words, 'holy, holy, holy', in the Kedushah during the repetition of the Amidah, and it is a custom to rise on the toes at each 'holy'.

chat.says: What does hineni mean, and why does Isaiah's hineni stand out?
options: Here I am. Isaiah says it to an open question, before he even hears the task.
It means I'm not worthy; Isaiah says it to turn the call down.
It means holy; the seraphim sing it, and Isaiah joins in with them.
chat.meaning: Abraham and Moses said hineni when called by name; Isaiah heard an open question, stepped forward, and said yes before he knew the job.

notes: Kedushah custom of rising on the toes: please confirm wording.
